Cancer survival in the United States has improved markedly over the past half-century: the overall 5-year relative survival rate for all cancers combined has climbed from roughly 49% for diagnoses in the mid-1970s to about 69% today, thanks to better screening, earlier detection, and advances in treatment such as targeted therapy and immunotherapy. That average, however, conceals enormous variation — some cancers are now largely curable while others remain stubbornly lethal, and rare cancers in particular often lag behind because they attract less research funding and are frequently diagnosed late.

1. Adrenocortical carcinoma — roughly 300 new cases per year in the US (about 1 case per million people)
2. Merkel cell carcinoma — roughly 2,500 new cases per year in the US
3. Gallbladder cancer — roughly 5,000 new cases per year in the US (about 12,000 if bile duct cancers are included)
4. Vulvar cancer — roughly 6,900 new cases per year in the US
5. Hodgkin lymphoma — roughly 8,500 new cases per year in the US
